subject: China-Kazakhstan renewable-energy investment and its political framing
original_lines: Kazakhstan’s transition to renewable energy has seen a significant surge in recent years. This rapidly growing green transition has allowed the country to meet its interim renewable-energy targets.

By 2030, Kazakhstan aims to generate 15 percent of its total energy output through renewables and increase this share to 50 percent by 2050. Kazakhstan has committed to reaching carbon neutrality by 2060.
The biggest partner in this endeavor has been China, whose role in the renewable-energy transition has grown and diversified over the years.
For Kazakhstan, the benefits of this partnership are clear: industrialization of its economy and, more importantly, decreasing carbon emissions and improving air quality and public health.

For China, the benefits go beyond lucrative investments and exporting its renewable-energy technology and include gaining soft power and offsetting its environmentally destructive footprint in Kazakhstan.

In addition to oil and gas resources, Kazakhstan has vast renewable-energy potential because of its large territory and abundance of wind and sunny days. It is the ninth largest country by area and holds 77 percent of Central Asia’s solar potential and 90 percent of the regional wind potential.
The presence of wind corridors in the Kazakh steppes makes Kazakhstan ideal for the operation of wind turbines. At least 50 percent of Kazakhstan’s territory is suitable for installing solar panels.

Most of the renewable-energy potential remains untapped. In 2024, 66 percent of Kazakhstan’s electricity was generated through coal, 21 percent through natural gas, 6.6 percent through hydroelectricity, and 6.4 percent through renewables.
Air pollution is a nationwide problem in Kazakhstan. In 2025, 35 cities faced significant air pollution, according to the National Hydrometeorological Service of Kazakhstan.
A major source of this pollution pandemic is coal burned by thermal power plants, industrial complexes, and households.

The list of adverse effects of air pollution is long. According to doctor Denis Vinnikov, long-term exposure increases the risk of cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
Almaty is one of the most polluted cities in Kazakhstan and is one of the national leaders with the highest cases of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
China is one of Kazakhstan’s largest trade and investment partners. Between 2005 and 2023, China invested over USD 25 billion in Kazakhstan.
Since 2018, Universal Energy has built 10 renewable-energy plants, three solar and seven wind, with a total capacity of 630 megawatts by winning government tenders.

State-owned Chinese companies have secured contracts through intergovernmental negotiations. The Zhanatas and Shelek wind power plants are operational, and five more renewable-energy plants are in development with a total capacity of 2.6 GW.
China’s investments in renewables are aimed at tackling concerns by gaining soft power and improving its reputation.
Renewable-energy projects allow Chinese companies to export excess capacity to foreign markets and may help China create a favorable perception abroad.
